groups.name: thegentlemen
groups.about: The Gentlemen is a ransomware-as-a-service group that emerged in July–August 2025 and quickly claimed over 320 victims in 17+ countries. It offers affiliates a 90% revenue share and uses a Go-based locker against Windows, Linux, NAS, and BSD. A 2026 compromised C2 server revealed over 1,570 linked victims.

groups.name: qilin
groups.about: Qilin ransomware was first observed in July 2022. It is written in Golang and offers multiple encryption modes that the operator controls. The group uses double extortion, demanding payment for a decryptor and for not releasing stolen data.

groups.name: incransom
groups.about: INC Ransom is a prolific ransomware-as-a-service operation active since July 2023. It targets healthcare, government, education, and manufacturing in North America and Europe, with no sector excluded. It posted over 200 victims in 2025 alone.

groups.name: safepay
groups.about: SafePay emerged in September 2024 and grew rapidly while rejecting the RaaS model, running all operations in-house. It claimed over 300 victims worldwide by mid-2025. An early high-profile attack on UK telematics firm Microlise reportedly stole 1.2 TB of data.

groups.name: akira
groups.about: Akira reportedly emerged in March 2023 and has been speculated to have ties to the former Conti group. Its affiliates reportedly also work with Snatch and BlackByte. The first version was written in C++ and later versions in Rust. Initial access has involved brute-force attacks on Cisco VPNs and exploitation of two CVEs.

groups.name: silentransomgroup
groups.about: Silentransomgroup is described in the notes as a former Conti team, also tracked as Chatty Spider and UNC3753. The notes give no further details on its operations or targets.

groups.name: rhysida
groups.about: Rhysida is a ransomware-as-a-service group that emerged in May 2023. It uses phishing and Cobalt Strike to breach networks and deploy its payload. It threatens to publish stolen data, leaves PDF notes, and accepts Bitcoin. The notes say the ransomware is still in early development.

groups.name: medusalocker
groups.about: The notes describe Medusa as a DDoS bot written in .NET 2.0, not a ransomware group. Its current command-and-control uses HTTP, while its predecessor used IRC. The notes do not describe ransomware activity, so this entry may be mislabeled.

groups.name: everest
groups.about: Everest collects and analyzes information about its victims, focusing on customer privacy, financial data, databases, and credit card information. It leaks stolen data on the darknet. It threatens to leak data and keep victims' files if they do not make contact.

groups.name: aurora
groups.about: Aurora is ransomware associated with a multi-purpose Go-based malware in use since mid-2022. Multiple criminal teams distribute it, and it is also sold on underground forums as an infostealer and botnet under the same name.

groups.name: braincipher
groups.about: Brain Cipher emerged in July 2024 with both Windows and Linux variants. It reportedly uses a leaked LockBit Black build and is suspected of exploiting CVE-2023-28252. Demands start at $150,000 and are paid in Monero. In 2025 it moved its negotiation portal to a new server.

groups.name: lockbit5
groups.about: LockBit 5.0, also called ChuongDong, emerged in September 2025 after the February 2024 law enforcement takedown of LockBit. It introduced cross-platform payloads targeting Windows, Linux, and VMware ESXi. It continues the RaaS affiliate model of its predecessors.

groups.name: metaencryptor
groups.about: Ransomware group first observed in mid-2023. Targets medium-to-large enterprises in legal, technology, logistics, manufacturing, and finance, mainly in the UK, Europe, and Southeast Asia. Uses AES-256 and RSA-2048 encryption with double extortion.

groups.name: payload
groups.about: Payload emerged in early 2026 and uses Babuk-derived source code to attack Windows and ESXi systems with double extortion. It targets healthcare, energy, real estate, and agriculture. It claimed 12 victims across seven countries within hours of launching its leak site.

groups.name: everstake
groups.about: The notes say this group is not affiliated with Everstake, Inc., a legitimate blockchain infrastructure company. They suggest the group may be misusing that company's name. The notes give no details on when it appeared, how it operates, or who it targets.

Okay, great. So the same sensitive data needs one security tool in Chrome and another in Slack? One for Edge and another for WhatsApp?

Same data. Same actions. Same risks.

Are we sure it needs a different security stack?

93% of the top 200 applications run on browser-based surfaces, embed a browser, or embed AI. The line between "browser security" and "desktop security" is getting harder to defend.

Different wrapper. Same web session underneath.

After Hugging Face there was this silly discourse about how you can't do anything against zero-day exploits.

Assume you have one of those enterprise gateway/firewall appliances that have zero-days found in their web management interfaces every other week.

For arguments sake, I'm going to simply accept that you can't take the management interface offline. You can't configure it to be accessible only from the local network. It has to be accessible to anyone connecting from anywhere.

The overwhelming majority of threat actors (including state-sponsored ones) tend to be overly reliant on internet scanning. They use services like Shodan/Censys, which scan every IPv4 address, then create indexes listing all the devices they find.

Threat actors then come along, use a search query to export a list of "<insert appliance type> by <insert vendor>", then either mass-exploit them, or pick and choose the devices belonging to organizations they're interested in.

One option: Create a subdomain, ideally something not easily guessable like "firewall-​a4f8d5.​yourcompany​.com". 

Sign up for a proxy/CDN provider like Cloudflare or similar. Configure the provider to forward traffic designated for that domain to the public IP address of your appliance, then enable revere proxy mode.

Now, go into your firewall and set up a rule to block all access to the management interface from IPs not belonging to Cloudflare. Either with an CIDR or ASN allow list.

Your device now doesn't show up in any internet scans at all, including those provided by Shodan or Censys, and the device is not directly accessible via IP address. But it is still accessible to anyone with the domain.

You've now reduced your blast radius from "every zero-day (or n-day if you don't patch immediately) is rocking my device" to "99.9% of exploitation attempts don't even see it", all without sacrificing availability.

Highly targeted attacker may go to the extra effort of figuring out the subdomain you use, and try to exploit the devices through the reverse proxy. But the way reverse proxies work breaks a lot of exploits, and Web Application Firewalls add a layer of additional protection.

Techniques like this work for most web-based appliances (which tend to get hit a lot as the result of internet scans). And there are plenty of simple things you can do for other software/devices which massively reduces your attack surface. Just one extra layer between the attacker and the target works wonders.

The whole "zero-day exploits are unstoppable" attitude is extremely defeatists, and also extremely wrong. Ask your friendly neighborhood blue teamer or threat intelligence professional for attack surface reduction advice.

digest.overview: Active exploitation of Azure, SAP NetWeaver and VMware dominates, alongside a critical npm RCE flaw, extortion-group activity and several data breaches.

themes.title: Exploited SAP NetWeaver and VMware vCenter flaws
themes.summary: The Hacker News, citing Onapsis, says attackers are actively exploiting SAP NetWeaver flaw CVE-2025-42884 with no public exploit available. Onapsis warns it could allow remote code execution, and the post urges patching now. The same outlet's roundup also reports a VMware vCenter zero-day (CVSS 9.8) as exploited, without a CVE ID.

themes.title: Azure flaw exploited to steal API credentials
themes.summary: BleepingComputer reports attackers exploited a Microsoft Azure flaw to steal customers' API credentials. SecurityWeek and The Record both say it affected Norwegian energy firms Equinor and Skagerak Energi, which Norway's cybersecurity authorities confirmed. A separate post flags a related Azure API Management secrets leak. No CVE is named.

themes.title: Critical npm binary-parser code execution flaw
themes.summary: The Hacker News reports a 9.2-severity flaw in the npm library binary-parser, CVE-2026-134814, which can let attackers run arbitrary JavaScript in Node.js apps. It affects versions before 2.3.1 when attackers control parser definitions. SANS ISC also lists it. Related coverage describes a phpAfterShell flaw that revives the PHP2Shell attack path.

themes.title: Data breaches at KEPCO, NCIC and N-able
themes.summary: BleepingComputer reports South Korea's KEPCO confirmed a data breach affecting 1.5 million people. The Record says the FBI is reportedly investigating a breach of the National Crime Information Center database. SecurityWeek reports a critical N-able flaw patched after a Mail Assure cyberattack. These posts cover separate incidents.

themes.title: Extortion groups target organizations and claim Nvidia breach
themes.summary: ESET says the Gentlemen ransomware-as-a-service group claimed an attack on Nvidia, and that the Tox ID used may point to direct involvement by the operators. ESET has seen no evidence yet to back the claim. Unit 42 reports an active campaign using legal-themed domains, some linked to the newly named extortion brand Inception and to Com-affiliated actors.

points.title: Synology DSM output encoding flaw
points.why: Confirmed exploited and used in ransomware campaigns; added to KEV within the last week, so patch now.

points.title: Google Brotli unchecked return value flaw
points.why: Confirmed exploited; exploitation within the next 30 days is predicted to be near-certain.

points.title: Barracuda ESG authentication bypass flaw
points.why: Confirmed exploited authentication bypass on email security gateways, added to KEV within the last two weeks.
